column1: What is the Pareto efficiency criterion?
column2: An allocation is Pareto efficient if no reallocation can make at least one individual strictly better off without making any other individual strictly worse off. It makes no claim about fairness or justice.

column1: In an Edgeworth box, what condition defines a point on the contract curve?
column2: Tangency between individual A's and B's indifference curves, i.e., equalized marginal rates of substitution: MRS_A^XY = MRS_B^XY.

column1: Why is an allocation with MRS_A^XY = 3 and MRS_B^XY = 1 not Pareto efficient?
column2: A trade exists (at an exchange ratio between 1 and 3) that makes both parties strictly better off, since A values X more highly relative to Y than B does, so mutually beneficial exchange is still possible.

column1: What is the classical utilitarian social welfare function and its key assumption?
column2: W^U = Σ u_i (sum of individual utilities). It assumes utilities are interpersonally comparable and cardinally measurable.

column1: What is the Rawlsian alternative to utilitarian social welfare aggregation?
column2: Maximin reasoning: society should maximize the welfare of the worst-off individual, derived from rational choice behind a 'veil of ignorance' about one's position in the distribution.

column1: What is the Kaldor-Hicks criterion (potential Pareto improvement)?
column2: A policy is an improvement if aggregate benefits B exceed aggregate costs C (B > C), regardless of who bears the costs and who receives the benefits—compensation is hypothetical, not actual.

column1: What is the Scitovsky double criterion and why is it needed?
column2: It requires both the Kaldor test (A→B) and the Hicks test (no reversal from B→A) to be satisfied simultaneously, because the Kaldor criterion alone can produce logical cycles/reversals under non-convexity or strong income effects.

column1: What is the core assumption set required for the First Fundamental Welfare Theorem to hold?
column2: Complete markets, perfect information, price-taking behavior, and the absence of externalities—when any fails, competitive equilibrium no longer guarantees Pareto efficiency.

column1: How does a negative production externality create inefficiency? (e.g., factory pollution)
column2: The firm sets P = C'(q) (private marginal cost), but social efficiency requires P = C'(q) + D'(q) (social marginal cost including damage). The wedge D'(q) causes overproduction whenever D'(q) > 0.

column1: What two properties define a pure public good?
column2: Non-rivalry (one person's consumption doesn't diminish availability to others) and non-excludability (no one can be prevented from consuming it), e.g., national defense or lighthouse signals.

column1: What is the traffic congestion externality mechanism?
column2: Each driver considers only private travel time, ignoring the incremental delay imposed on all other vehicles; marginal social cost exceeds private cost, causing peak-hour traffic to exceed the socially optimal flow and generating deadweight loss.

column1: What normative trade-off is embedded in using Kaldor-Hicks CBA for policy evaluation?
column2: It licenses policies that impose real, uncompensated losses on identifiable people if justified by aggregate willingness-to-pay arithmetic, deliberately separating efficiency evaluation from distributional concerns (left to tax-and-transfer systems).
